/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.headline: Monday briefing: Can we change the system that protects men like Russell Brand?
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.excerpt: Good morning. Later today, Russell Brand will be sentenced at Southwark crown court in London after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others in separate incidents committed at the very height of his fame. The trial judge has already warned Brand, a comedian and actor turned social activist then Christian influencer, to expect “a significant custodial term”. The rape he will be sentenced for is one of the 9% of cases to make it from police report to court last year and, of those, one of 53% that result in a conviction. Let that sit with you for a few moments: the justice done and the context in which justice is done. Because the context around Brand’s offending is everything: the media circus, the tired tropes, the threats of litigation, the enablers and the institutional cultures of silence that protect powerful perpetrators. These all make it harder to expose predators and secure convictions. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to senior reporter Emine Sinmaz and comedian Kate Smurthwaite about the trial and its aftershocks. But first the weekend’s headlines. Weekend roundup Poland | Six people were killed and 16 wounded after a gunman opened fire with a semiautomatic weapon in a busy market square in Kraków on Saturday, in what authorities are calling “an act of terror”.
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.trail: In today’s newsletter: ​Justice has been done for some of Russell Brand’s victims but the courts and the entertainment industry must do more to stop powerful men taking advantage of a culture that enables their behaviour

/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.headline: Russell Brand case must be wake-up call to protect women in media, Lisa Nandy says
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.excerpt: The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said there is still a problem with exploitation and abuse in the media industry and a failure to properly deal with allegations after Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault. She said women who came forward were too often not protected by institutions across public life, including in politics, and that huge power imbalances meant speaking up came at a very heavy cost. Nandy told the media industry that “time is up” to bring in systems to protect vulnerable whistleblowers, and said that while the BBC had taken action in recent years, other organisations still had to take the problem seriously. Brand’s conviction on Thursday renewed scrutiny of how the UK’s entertainment industry has treated celebrities accused of abusing their power, with some women saying they feared that speaking out could harm their careers. Brand faces sentencing on Monday after being found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others. The judge said he faces a “significant” prison term. Nandy said last week that the case must be a wake-up call to the media world and beyond, after widespread concerns over failures to confront Brand’s behaviour. It emerged after the verdicts that he is under investigation for two further rape allegations. In an interview with the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy was asked if she thought there was still a problem in the media and creative industries.
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.trail: Culture secretary says there is still a problem with exploitation and abuse in the industry and public life

/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.headline: Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.excerpt: Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star. Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years. The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials. The Guardian also understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims. The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system. Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum. The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material. Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating.
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.trail: Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing

/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-hu.headline: Trump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’
/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-hu.excerpt: Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives. “It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week. “The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests.
/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-hu.trail: The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’

/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.headline: Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’
/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.excerpt: The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military. Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates. The defense secretary pointed to those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. About “80% of the force” onboard was retained, he said. Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration. “The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.” He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals.
/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.trail: Amid latest extraordinary attack on diversity, US defense secretary also suggests military is retaining service personnel at ‘record’ rates

/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.headline: House speaker calls early recess before midterms amid AI regulation frenzy
/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.excerpt: The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. It’s the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday. “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump. “We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday.
/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.trail: Mike Johnson cancels votes on Thursday, meaning House members will avoid voting on impeaching Pete Hegseth

/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.headline: Trump the environmentalist? How his Iran war exposed the fragility of dirty energy
/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.excerpt: Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist. Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran. “He’s woken the world up to how vulnerable we are to petro-dictatorships, how vulnerable we are to disruptions in the Middle East,” Newsom told the Guardian during Climate Week in New York. “This war has completely gutted any sort of romantic notions of energy security and it’s compelled folks to think differently. It’s accelerating investments and clean energy and renewables.” If Trump has been an accidental environmentalist, it’s been in the international sphere. The strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports usually flow, is now starting to open up but has been routinely snarled since the Iran war began in February, causing the cost of these fossil fuels to soar around the world. Countries reacted by scrambling to cut their oil and gas use while turning to cleaner forms of energy such as solar and wind (although there’s also been a small rise in coal, the dirtiest of fossil fuels). The overall consequence has been a positive one for our shared climate, with global fossil fuel emissions set to drop by 0.5% this year due to the crisis, Carbon Brief has estimated.
/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.trail: Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security

/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.headline: China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed
/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.excerpt: China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows. The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy. China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February. How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand. The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport.
/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.trail: Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls

/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.headline: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.excerpt: More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal. The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official. It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”. NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024.
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.trail: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official

/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.headline: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.excerpt: NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases. Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”. The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces.
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.trail: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use

/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.headline: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.excerpt: Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology. The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue. Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months. Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027. David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes.
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.trail: Exclusive: Campaign comes amid backlash against tech company’s involvement with Israeli military and Trump’s ICE crackdown

/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.headline: ‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health minister
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.excerpt: Concern is being raised about Palantir’s work with the NHS as new figures showed tens of thousands of patients have withdrawn their data from use in research projects. James Frith, the health innovation minister, said he was worried about “mistrust” of the US defence and health tech company and “the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”. The government is deciding whether to axe the company’s £330m contract to operate the health service’s federated data platform, which is intended to improve efficiency and patient outcomes. Frith’s comment, in a letter to Layla Moran, the chair of the Commons health committee, follows a rise in patients opting out of allowing their medical data to be shared. In the two months from mid-May to mid-July, 60,000 more people withdrew their private information under a mechanism called the national data opt-out. Doctors and patients’ groups are calling for Labour to exercise a break clause in Palantir’s seven-year contract. They cite its work with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration agency and question the company’s claim to provide value for money. Palantir and its supporters say its AI-driven technology has cut NHS waiting lists for surgery.
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.trail: James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs

/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.headline: ‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power couple
/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.excerpt: The literary power couple is a historically seductive concept. Two writers sharing a life, their private and creative worlds entwined, each becoming witness to and critic of the other’s work. Think Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre, Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne. Or, less auspiciously, Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes. Now, into this illustrious company steps a new pair: the novelist Marlon James and the biographer Nicholas Boggs, whose books have each been shortlisted for one of Britain’s most prestigious literary awards – James for the Booker prize and Boggs for the Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction. Between them, they have produced two formidable books, each the culmination of years of work, and each concerned with the lives of Black queer men whose stories have often been overlooked. “I’m not sure what to do with it,” James says, when I ask how they feel about the inevitable impending “literary power couple” label. “I have all these romantic notions that we were like Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne or something – I don’t know. What do you think?” He turns to Boggs, who laughs. “It’s all very new,” he says. “We’re still getting used to it.” It is a warm October morning in Williamsburg, the fashionable writerly enclave in Brooklyn, and I am sitting across from the pair at their apartment. They are relaxing on a chaise longue, looking comfortable enough to have been there all morning.
/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.trail: Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history

/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.headline: Previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart shortlisted for Booker prize
/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.excerpt: This year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison. Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November. James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time for The Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list. Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in a Guardian review. Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William!
/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.trail: The two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelist

/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.headline: Peter Asher: Everywhere Man review – music-biz face from Beatles-buddy pop act to superstar producer
/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.excerpt: Rock’n’roll is notorious for its tales of bad behaviour: throwing TVs out of the window, mountains of cocaine, parades of groupies … but you won’t find any of that here. Peter Asher, brother of Jane, one half of Peter and Gordon, and super-successful producer of acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt, appears to be about as nerdish and clean-living as a 60s/70s music industry veteran could be. Although that might just be what he wants us to think; what are the chances Asher is a complete reprobate away from the camera, and is just brilliant at hiding it? That glasses and ruffled shirt front combo definitely reminds you of someone a tad more sleazy, even before Asher himself reminds you about it in the final credits. Whatever the truth, Asher by any standards carved an amazing path through it all, making the absolute most of being in the right place at the right time. Smartly structured around Asher’s current anecdotes-and-music live show, the film stitches together a collection of clips, audio and musical performances that gallops through his personal backstory.
/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.trail: Backstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt

/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.headline: Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028
/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.excerpt: Liverpool is to unveil a new 100,000 sq ft visitor attraction about the Beatles, in plans hailed as “extraordinary” by Paul McCartney, and by Andy Burnham as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain”. Opening in 2028, the project is a huge upgrade for the Beatles Story, a museum which opened in Liverpool’s Royal Albert Dock in 1990. Ownership will now pass to the Beatles company Apple Corps, making the Beatles Story the band’s first official fan experience in their home city. It will also move across the city to the former shopping centre St John’s Market, close to Liverpool’s Lime Street railway station, which has lain unused since closing in 2024. The new site will allow the museum to become four times bigger than its current home. Apple Corps has also announced it will take over and renovate Liverpool’s second-tallest building: St Johns Beacon, a 450ft tower that has also remained unused since 2024, when its viewing gallery closed and its radio station tenants vacated. Neighbouring the redeveloped museum, the tower will become a separate attraction themed around the Beatles’ whimsical and psychedelic animated film Yellow Submarine.
/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.trail: City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building
